title: Reading For Change: Resources for Place-Based Systems Change
content:
The Place Project was a place-based systems change project in lutruwita/Tasmania. It was funded by the Paul Ramsay Foundation and the Tasmanian Community Fund and auspiced by Burnie Works. From 2024 it brought together people from Burnie, Devonport, kinimathatakinta/George Town, Brighton and Clarence Plains, as well as a multicultural place-based stream. The project wrapped up at the end of September 2026.

We set out to learn what makes place-based work succeed in Tasmania and what each community knows and does in its own way.

We set out to learn what makes place-based work succeed in Tasmania and what each community knows and does in its own way.

The original plan didn’t last long once communities got involved. The project was reshaped by the people in it, through community-hosted Gatherings, rapid co-design sessions and a Sense Making Day. Along the way, people stopped waiting to be asked and started leading.

title: Real Problems, Real Solutions: A Messaging Guide to Move Beyond Racial Scapegoating in the Victorian Election
content:
This message guide has been developed by Common Cause Australia in partnership with the Asylum Seeker Resource Centre and Democracy in Colour, with additional input from GetUp, Victorian Trades Hall Council, and Australian Progress.

This is an interim guide based on early research with persuadable audiences carried out by Common Cause Australia as part of a larger forthcoming project on framing migration in Australia. It is designed for organisations communicating with the public in the run-up to the Victorian Election in November 2026. In addition to our own early research, this interim guide draws on research carried out by GetUp, Victorian Trades Hall Council and ACTU, who kindly shared recent insights.

During elections, debates about migration, multiculturalism, refugees and people seeking asylum can become particularly heightened. Racial scapegoating and divisive rhetoric can become more prominent in public debate.

title: Scenario Planning: Civil Society Responses to Far Right Authoritarianism
content:
This is a scenario planning tool for civil society organisations concerned about whether they have the right strategies in place given the rise of the authoritarian far right and the influence it is already having.

The tool was developed by Jim Coe, UK social movement researcher and consultant. Jim Coe and Natasha Adams have convened gatherings; undertaken research; and produced reports investigating the impact of the far right on civil society organisations, and the range of potential responses.

In their report, Towards Meaningful Action: NGOs’ responses to threats from far-right authoritarianism, Coe and Adams emphasise the need to take substantive steps across a range of areas: Building a collective response; Organisations’ capabilities and preparedness; and Organisational strategy.

The problem we are facing is that a far-right, authoritarian political party is increasingly gaining access to power and could potentially form a future government, but also that the influence of the far-right is already permeating government and other policy, discourse, and spaces for influence. – Towards Meaningful Action, 2026

title: WTF: the Rise of the Tech Broligarchy
content:
MediaJustice presented a political education series to help activists understand the ‘tech broligarchy’. Please note the series ran from February to May 2025 and some details may be out of date. However, it remains a valuable overview of the dynamics shaping economics and politics in the US and globally.

In Trump’s first 100 days in office, the tech bro executives— who we call the Tech Broligarchy — proudly flaunted their corporate-state collusion to surveil, criminalize, and control us for profit. From Musk’s DOGE purging federal agencies and workers that might regulate his businesses to Palantir’s overlooked role in scaling mass ICE raids and daylight abductions, these Broligarchs are directly executing policy that only benefit themselves while undermining our democracy.

MediaJustice’s WTF: The Rise of the Tech Broligarchy Toolkit is a companion resource to the seven-part political education webinar series, which exposes and resists these tech billionaires and their agenda during Trump’s first 100 days in office and beyond. Download the toolkit to bring these conversations into your communities and build our collective power against the Tech Broligarchy.

title: Weaving the Threads Together: How to Document Your Campaign
content:
Resources from a webinar by the Commons Library and the Leading Change Network (LCN) about learning how to document your organizing and campaigning.

Documentation is not a luxury; it’s a movement necessity.

Documentation is not a luxury; it’s a movement necessity.

When was the last time you documented your organizing campaign – the ups and the downs, the stories, the lessons learned?

Behind every campaign, there is a journey of courage, collaboration, struggles, victories, and deep learning. But too often, those stories and learnings fade once the moment passes. What if we could preserve them? Pass them on? Use them to teach, to inspire, and to build stronger movements!

title: Guide to Artivism in Exile: Between Expression, Struggle, and Societal Transformation
content:
The toolkit is intended primarily for artists, cultural workers, and artistic collectives living or working in exile, migration, and diaspora, and assumes no particular academic background or artistic discipline. It is equally applicable to facilitators developing artivism workshops, to cultural and human rights organisations, residency programmes, and funders working with displaced artists, and to researchers examining art, migration, resistance, and social change.

This toolkit gives artists in exile the analytical tools to decide for themselves what the political dimension of their work will be. – Source

title: How to Stop a Data Centre in Australia
content:
Resources gathered by The Commons librarians to support local communities organising and campaigning against AI Data Centres. It was initially put together to inform participants at the Community Summit in Naarm/Melbourne on 5 September 2026.

It can be daunting to go up against entrenched government and corporate power – but people power can prevail!

Here in Australia we can learn from the history of community activism in this country, as well as struggles and innovations overseas. We don’t need to reinvent the wheel. We can learn together and share lessons as campaigns evolve.

This guide is a work in progress. It builds on our international resource, How to Stop a Data Centre: Tools for Community Resistance. We welcome feedback and suggestions for inclusion: Contact us.

From past experience and the expressed needs of people involved in these fights, we believe the following areas of knowledge and skills are crucial.

  • Know about Data Centres
  • Know about the specific Data Centre project you want to stop 
  • Engage the Community 
  • Organise Locally 
  • Plan a Strategic Campaign
  • Tell the Story
  • Take Action 
  • Reflect and Adapt 
  • Collaborate Across the Movement

title: Talking When We Disagree – Download Free Guide
content:
It starts with having better conversations.

Many of us have experienced conversations that quickly become tense, or we have avoided them altogether for fear of conflict, misunderstanding or damaging a relationship. But social change has always depended on people being able to build relationships, listen deeply and engage with those who do not see the world the same way they do.

This guide brings together some of our favourite Commons Library resources on navigating difficult conversations, building unlikely coalitions and strengthening solidarity in divided times. Whether you are looking for practical conversation techniques, examples of deep canvassing or lessons from movements that have successfully organised across difference, these resources offer both inspiration and practical tools.

Sign up to The Commons Social Change Library newsletter to get your free guide – Talking When We Disagree: How to Talk about Sensitive Topics, featuring practical tools for navigating disagreement, building understanding and organising across difference.

title: Striking Voices: Young People and Climate Justice
content:
The Striking Voices project is a transgenerational participatory project about climate justice, young people’s collective advocacy, and the role of education in times of escalating, overlapping injustices.

This four year project (2022-2026), with four younger climate justice organisers employed as Research Associates, has involved storytelling and creative-making processes, with other young (12-24 years old) climate justice organisers, their mentors, and secondary school teachers, about their experiences of climate justice activism/advocacy/organising and education.

The project has been funded by the Australian Research Council (DE220100103; 2022-2026) and Deakin University.

title: Funny Climate Activism? An Analysis of Creative Digital Action by Young People
content:
The following is a summary and excerpts from the article ‘Funny climate activism? A collaborative storied analysis of young climate advocates’ digital activisms’. It was originally published in the journal Global Studies of Childhood in 2024 and was written by Sophie Chiew, Eve Mayes, Netta Maiava, Dani Villafaña and Natasha Abhayawickrama. These five researchers are associated with Striking Voices, a participatory research project exploring how young people in Australia use activism, creative storytelling, and education to fight for climate justice. Four of the authors are 19 to 22 years old and involved in climate justice organizing and one is a university-based researcher in their early 40s.

In the face of intersecting injustices, humour has the potential to enliven and sustain collective solidarity. Collective work towards climate justice feels good when ‘wacky’ actions are done together, stereotypes and affinities are laughed at… and false forms of liberation… are satirised. – Chiew, Mayes, Maiava, Villafaña and Abhayawickrama, 2024
